title: The Kiss in the Storeroom
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 27 of 40
content:
The first time Severus Snape kissed me, we were arguing about powdered unicorn horn.

I wish that were more dignified.

It was not.

The hearing was the next morning. Neither of us had slept. Rather than admit this, we had gone to the dungeon before sunrise to complete a stock transfer that could easily have waited a week.

I was checking a shipment from Diagon Alley.

Snape was correcting me.

“This grade is unacceptable.”

“The supplier lists it as medicinal.”

“The supplier is either lying or blind.”

I held the packet under the lamp.

“It looks fine.”

“It is too coarse.”

“It's powder.”

“It is gravel pretending to be powder.”

“You're nervous.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Do not change the subject.”

“You're bullying unicorn horn because you're nervous.”

“I am identifying substandard material.”

“Personally.”

“Unlike you, I take standards seriously.”

There it was.

The cheap cut.

Not as cruel as the letter day.

Still deliberate.

I set down the packet.

“Try again.”

His expression changed.

“What?”

“You're afraid. Fine. You're angry. Fine. You want to complain about the supplier until sunrise, also fine. You don't get to use me as a practice target.”

His jaw tightened.

“I did not—”

“Yes, you did.”

Silence.

The old pattern stood between us like an open door.

He could deny.

Escalate.

Make me prove the injury before he acknowledged it.

Instead Snape closed his eyes.

“You are right.”

The anger drained out of me so quickly it left me tired.

“I hate when you do that.”

His eyes opened.

“Apologize?”

“Improve.”

His mouth twitched.

“I am sorry.”

“Thank you.”

We stood on opposite sides of the storeroom.

It was narrow, lined floor to ceiling with jars and packets. One lamp hung overhead. The air smelled of dried herbs, stone, and the faint metallic sweetness of unicorn horn.

Snape rubbed his hand over his face.

“I should not be here.”

“At Hogwarts?”

“In this room.”

“Because of the horn?”

“Because I am tired enough to be careless.”

I softened.

“Then let's stop.”

He looked at me.

“Just like that?”

“Yes.”

“The inventory—”

“Will survive.”

“The hearing—”

“Will happen whether these shelves are finished or not.”

He leaned back against the wall.

For once, Snape looked exactly as tired as he was.

I stepped closer.

Not too close.

“Do you want company?” I asked.

His gaze lifted.

“Yes.”

So I leaned against the opposite shelf.

We stood there, two exhausted adults hiding from a government hearing between jars of beetle eyes.

It was ridiculous.

I began to laugh.

Snape looked offended.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Do not.”

“Tomorrow, half the Wizengamot is going to debate your soul, and right now you're sulking next to dried nettles.”

His mouth twitched.

“When phrased by an idiot, most situations sound absurd.”

“There you are.”

He laughed.

Softly.

The tension broke.

Then didn't.

Because when the laughter faded, we were still looking at each other.

Still too awake.

Too aware.

Weeks of almost-touch lived in the small room with us.

His fingers on my cheek.

My mouth against his knuckles.

Three steps under an umbrella.

A hand held across a table marked by old allegiance.

Snape's eyes dropped to my mouth.

This time he did not immediately look away.

My pulse changed.

He heard the shift in my breathing.

“You are doing that again,” he said.

“What?”

“Looking at me as though I am about to become someone else.”

“I don't want someone else.”

The words came easily.

His face changed.

“I know what you are,” I continued. “As much as anyone can. I know what you've done. I know what you regret. I know you're capable of being cruel when frightened. I know you hate sweet tea and sleep badly and alphabetize at home.”

His eyes narrowed.

“You swore never to weaponize that cupboard.”

“I made no such promise.”

“Untrustworthy.”

“Terribly.”

I stepped closer.

He did not move away.

“I don't want a nicer version of you,” I said.

“That is a foolish statement. I would prefer a nicer version of me.”

I laughed softly.

“Fine. I want you to become kinder. I don't want you to become generic.”

His mouth curved.

“An important distinction.”

“It is to me.”

The space between us narrowed.

Snape's hand rose.

He did not touch me.

“May I?”

“Yes.”

His fingers settled against my jaw.

The contact was familiar now.

The intention was not.

“May I kiss you?” he asked.

Every nerve in my body answered before my mouth did.

“Yes.”

He leaned in slowly.

For a man known for precision, the first contact was almost uncertain.

His mouth touched mine.

Soft.

Brief.

He pulled back half an inch.

I opened my eyes.

His were watching me.

“Again?” I whispered.

His breath caught.

“Yes?”

I smiled.

“Yes.”

The second kiss was different.

Still careful.

Not tentative.

His hand moved from my jaw to the back of my neck. Mine found the front of his coat, gripping fabric because I needed somewhere to put the sudden amount of feeling.

He kissed like he did most things once he committed: with concentrated attention.

No performance.

No hurry.

Every change asked through pause and pressure.

I answered by moving closer.

His back met the shelf.

A jar rattled.

We froze.

I laughed against his mouth.

Snape closed his eyes.

“If we die beneath pickled newts,” he murmured, “I will haunt you.”

“You'd haunt me anyway.”

“Probably.”

I kissed him again.

He made a low sound that traveled directly through me.

My hand rose toward his throat, then stopped.

The scar.

He felt the hesitation.

His eyes opened.

“Ask,” he said.

“Can I touch your neck?”

Fear flickered.

Then trust.

“Not the scar.”

“Okay.”

I let my fingertips rest against the uninjured side below his ear.

His pulse jumped beneath them.

He exhaled.

“Still all right?”

“Yes.”

The word was rough.

I kissed him more gently.

When we finally separated, neither of us looked particularly dignified.

Snape's hair had fallen across his face.

My coat was crooked.

The unicorn horn remained substandard.

He looked at the packet on the table.

“Still gravel,” he said.

I started laughing again.

He pressed his forehead briefly to mine.

That gesture almost affected me more than the kiss.

“What now?” I asked.

His expression sobered.

“Now we sleep.”

“Separately?”

Color rose at his cheeks.

I had not meant it as pressure, only a question.

“Yes,” he said.

“Okay.”

“And tomorrow—”

“We go to the hearing.”

“Yes.”

“Together?”

He looked at me.

Then held out his hand.

“Together.”

I took it.

We left the storeroom at sunrise.

The powdered unicorn horn stayed on the rejection pile.

Some standards, apparently, remained non-negotiable.
